speaker: Other
text: This is Supreme Court case number CRA20-009, People of Guam, Plaintiff Appellee versus Eric Juan Palacios Kitagwa, Defendant Appellant. Appearing for the Defendant Appellant is Attorney Heather M. Zona. Appearing for the Plaintiff Appellee is Attorney Jeremiah Luther. The panel consists of Chief Justice F. Philip Carbolito, Associate Justice Robert J. Torres, and Associate Justice Catherine A. Merriman. Attorney Zona reserves how many minutes? Seven minutes. Thank you. Seven minutes. And Attorney Luther has 15 minutes to argue. Thank you, Madam Clerk. Attorney Zona,

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: you are recognized and you may proceed. Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, Justice Torres, Justice Merriman, may it please the court. This interlocutory appeal addresses whether Mr. Kitagwa as an indigent defendant may apply to the trial court for expert assistance ex parte, under seal, without notice to the prosecution and general public, and without revealing his defense strategies. Or, as the trial court found, Mr. Kitagwa must first reveal his work product in the form of defense strategies to the prosecution and public at large in order to seek the tools for an adequate defense. We seek the following relief. First, a determination that an indigent defendant is not required to disclose his defense strategies to the prosecution and the general public in order to secure the constitutional guarantee to an adequate defense. And second, a determination that an indigent defendant may apply to the court for expert assistance ex parte, under seal, and without notice to the prosecution and the general public. The legal issue here is a narrow one, but one that implicates many areas of law, including constitutional rights, statutory rights, ethical obligations, and work product. And these issues are present in every case involving an indigent defendant. So the court's guidance on the issue here will provide clarification for all cases involving indigent defendants. It will avoid inconsistent results. And most importantly, it will protect the accused constitutional guarantees and his rights under Guam law. Now, with respect to the trial court order, the Superior Court found Mr. Kitagawa indigent, and that was made pursuant to Superior Court Rule MR 1.1. So Mr. Kitagawa's indigence is not at issue here. And it never was at issue once the court made that finding. But because Mr. Kitagawa is indigent, he has to apply to the Superior Court for financial assistance to secure expert assistance. And he also has to explain why that's necessary. And that's under the Rule MR 1.1.4. So Mr. Kitagawa did apply to the trial court ex parte under seal and without notice of the prosecution. And in accordance with Rule CVR 7.11, Mr. Kitagawa submitted a declaration explaining why notice of the application was not provided to the prosecution. And specifically, the reasons were number one, to avoid broadcasting his defense strategies. Number two, to avoid violating his due process and equal protection rights by conditioning receipt of the tools for an adequate defense on disclosure of his legal strategies. And number three, because permitting the prosecution to weigh in on his defense strategies and tactics in the form of seeking expert assistance would undermine both the attorney client privilege as well as Mr. Kitagawa's right to effective assistance of counsel pursuant to the Sixth Amendment. Mr. Kitagawa further requested that any order and offers of proof in connection with the request be made ex parte and that they be filed under seal to afford him that same

speaker: roberttorres
text: protection. The trial court... Ms. Silna, can I ask a question here? It seems that the prosecution has conceded that a request for an ex parte hearing to raise the substantive issues before the trial court in camera regarding the necessity of an expert in a particular case seems appropriate. But they argue that the mere act of noticing them that you're going forward with such a request doesn't fall within the protections of the work product doctrine. And they ask that we look at Georgia law where there's notice of public, you know, generally a notice of public filing of a notice about the request without any, you know, details, I guess, concerning the particular expert that's going to be sought and the reasons for it, etc. And just that, the amount of the funding that's going to be required to hire that expert. But you think that's still protected within the work product doctrine?

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: I do. And I'll tell you why, for a couple of reasons. Number one, there may very well be cases where simply the fact that somebody is seeking expert assistance reveals quite a bit in terms of strategy or weaknesses in case or whatnot that pertains to it. Number two, I do think that the act of seeking, deciding whether to seek expert assistance does fall within work product, because it does reveal a path that a defense may move along. So... How does that prejudice

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: a defendant? You make the general comment that just giving notice that the defendant is seeking an expert in some way divulges some type of strategy. But, you know, when a person pleads not guilty by reason of mental illness, for example, and seeking a psychiatrist expert, how is the mere... I don't know what was the plea here. I plead, I assume it's just not guilty, but how does just giving notice that the defendant is seeking an expert, and maybe without even divulging the type of expert that is being sought, prejudice the defendant or assist the government?

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: Well, there are different types of cases and experts can be sought in all kinds of different areas. And we'll concede that there are instances where it's quite obvious. I mean, I've been involved in a number of cases where it's very clear the government has a DNA expert and I'm going to get my own DNA expert. But there may be other instances where there's just simply the disclosure of the fact that there's an expert can reveal to the prosecution that there may be an issue that the prosecution may very well not have thought about, may very well not have pursued, or may not recognize that there's a particular...

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: You're asking us to do just a blanket rule. In all instances, the defendant doesn't matter what type of expert, whether it's a fingerprint expert, a psychiatrist expert, that the defendant not have to provide notice in a request for an ex parte hearing.

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: That's exactly right. Yes, Your Honor.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Let me just finish here. I'm sorry. Just saying generally that there may be conveying... Give me an example. I mean, if the defendant pleads not guilty by reason of mental illness, decides that he or she wants to then seek an expert witness, how would that... speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: Well, if not guilty for reason of mental illness, I mean, I think that that is perhaps not the best example for what I'm looking for because in that instance, I think it's clear to everyone that we would need psychiatric expert assistance on both sides. And I would imagine that the court...

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: I use that example as the first instance because you're asking us to do no exception across the board that the government not be provided notice. Well, I'll give the reasons of why you're asking for an expert.

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: Absolutely. So I would also clarify that what we've said in our briefing is that it's actually up to the defendant and the defendant's counsel to decide when to provide that notice. So it wouldn't preclude in a situation, as your honor pointed out, where there's not guilty by reason of insanity, that that wouldn't preclude the defendant from providing that notice. And certainly there are instances where a trial court judge would say, okay, counsel, this is the issue. I want you to disclose your expert by this date, this expert by the other date. We could have a situation, for example, perhaps there is a blood splatter analysis. Maybe there are no experts needed for perhaps a case, but it's very clear that there's blood splatter. And maybe the prosecution hasn't thought about that. And so providing notice that we're going to actually be looking at that, that could in fact, key up for the prosecution, the fact that there is that issue. But more importantly, the other issue in terms of prejudice could come out at trial. So for example, even in an instance where, for example, DNA were an issue and the prosecution clearly will have a DNA expert and the defense might not necessarily want to disclose right away that there's a DNA expert at trial by notifying that there will be an expert sought. I could, and I'm just using this as an example, I could talk to my DNA expert. The prosecution would know that I would have identified an expert, but they can probably figure out based on the facts. And then I don't call that expert at trial. So I would not want to have a situation where then at trial, the prosecution is able to argue, well, hey, they sought expert assistance. Where's their expert? Their expert isn't even here. And therefore you should side with us. That's an advantage that they would get that would prejudice my client that they would not necessarily have if they didn't know that there was an expert being sought. And this is by the way, the process in California, where I have practiced, we always would file our requests ex parte and under seal, except in a case, for example, where NGRI is an issue for exactly that reason. So again, it's not precluding notice to be given to the prosecution in an appropriate case. But I think that to say that there needs to be notice in every case sort of is backwards because it does create. So do we follow the jurisdiction that

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: leaves it to the discretionary of the trial judge to determine whether or not notice should be given or not? Or an ex parte, whether it should be an ex parte hearing or not? I think that with respect

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: to the notice, the judge at the end of the day has the ultimate authority to run the case. But I would say that in the first instance, it would be up to the defendant as to whether that notice should be given for those reasons that I just articulated. And the Georgia decision, the Brooks case, I believe it is that the prosecution cited, actually that relied a lot on the fact that whether the client's indigence was an issue. So the prosecution's arguments are based on cases that say, well, they should have noticed because they need to make sure that the client truly is indigent. But that was actually rejected in another case, the Moody case

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: that was cited by the prosecution. Well, what about the instance where the trial court disallowed the ex parte hearing without notice, but during the ex parte hearing determines that it would be helpful for the government to weigh in. If the government was not given prior notice, at least an expert was being sought, then wouldn't that just add to additional pre-trial delay and having to then notify the government, the government having to be given the time to respond to the judge's questions. Whereas if the government was provided notice without the reasons or which experts being sought, then the government at least can provide based on its knowledge of the facts of the case, any information to the trial court at an ex parte hearing in a written filing information that may be helpful in arriving at a decision.

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: Well, your honor, that question gives me some pause because I think just from a constitutional perspective, I don't think that the government should be weighing in on whether an indigent defendant receives expert assistance. I think that in order to do that, they would have to be weighing in on, I mean, because the defendant already is required to justify to the trial court why the expert is necessary. And then to have at that hearing, the prosecution weigh in as to whether that expert truly is necessary, I think is really a nullification of the accused's

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: constitutional rights. If we follow the Arizona courts and several other jurisdictions, they've already taken the position that there's no constitutional and in their case statutory right for a defendant to be entitled to an ex parte hearing when it is seeking

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: an expert witness at government expense. Well, your honor, I would disagree with those cases. I mean, if it's a statutory issue that still does not address the constitutional issue. So the defendant may not have that right based on a statute, which quite honestly, I would question the constitutionality of that. But the defendant still would have a right under the constitution, the United States. Well, the Arizona Supreme Court didn't

speaker: roberttorres
text: believe that to be the case. And as Justice Carbolito ruled, they said there was no constitutional right to ex parte hearing on the necessity of an expert. But if, I mean, you know, the situation may be different as of course, where indigency has already been established and where indigency has not been established. So in the process of making a claim for an expert witness, if part of that same motion, you're trying to assert that the defendant is indigent and entitled to, and hasn't qualified in yet. And is there requiring the court to make a determination on that? I mean, one would expect maybe that bright defense counsel like yourself might bifurcate that motion, but what happens if they come in and they don't? I mean, are you suggesting that the state can't make an argument about qualification or shouldn't be entitled to prove that the person is secreting assets and not showing the full representation of their

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: qualification for representation? Well, no, I think that the government always can be present at any determination as to a client's indigency. I mean, I think that's the right. Obviously the court has the ultimate ability to decide and determine whether someone is indigent. And I think in Guam, I can't speak to Arizona, but I think in Guam there's a fairly rigorous process. Probation is involved. There are forms that are filed under oath. I think we articulated that. So I think the government can always address that, but I do think that that is an issue that is separate from whether an indigent defendant receives expert assistance. So I would think that bifurcating that, I don't think that they have anything to do with each other in the grand scheme of things. I think indigency is simply a hurdle that the defendant has to pass in order to show that he's eligible for an expert paid for by the court. But it does concern me as well to consider having the prosecution aware that the indigent defendant is seeking expert assistance because certainly it doesn't go both ways, right? I mean, we as representatives of indigent defendants in court and counsel, we have no idea when the prosecution goes and consults with their experts. So I would be concerned, and I would imagine the prosecution should be concerned too, that if we do end up having a situation where the indigent defendant is required to disclose that and provide notice to the prosecution, I think as a matter of fundamental fairness, then the prosecution would be required to advise us when they consult with experts, retain experts. And I don't think that that is in keeping with work product protection certainly, but also in terms of adequate representation of clients and avoiding prejudicing the clients and a whole host of other issues, including just setting up a really very troublesome and thorny issue for courts to decide later on.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: So Ms. Zona, if we were to consider the line of cases, the jurisdictions that leave it to the discretion of the trial court that the defendant must make a showing as to why notice should not be provided to the government, to the people, what type of standards should we consider so that it is not an unfettered discretion, but there needs to be an application of appropriate standards that the trial judge should be guided by in making the determination? speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: I do. I would say, Your Honor, that at this point, there actually is that ability. So this is not an NGRI situation, for example,

speaker: philipcarbullido

speaker: heathermartinezzona
text: respect to the actual declaration filed with respect to notice. However, whenever the trial court receives, any trial court receives these materials, it is never simply just the notice. It's also the actual motion that is supposed to be something that articulates very specifically why the expert is necessary. And I think that, I mean, this has been my experience in many jurisdictions, that most trial courts are really aware of what the issues are in a particular case and can kind of make those determinations quite easily as to whether something really is necessary and certainly whether somebody has made that requisite showing. So you would object then,

speaker: philipcarbullido

I think that unless the defendant specifically agrees or provides notice himself, herself of the request, I don't think that the trial court should be disposing that, because I think for the reasons that we've articulated, I think that it's a constitutional violation. speaker: jeremiahluther
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, Justice Torres, Justice Merriman. May it please the court. The government's position is quite clear on this. We agree with defense counsel that an indigent defendant has the right to keep defense strategy secret from the prosecution and application for funds for an expert. I believe that the case law on this issue is fairly overwhelming. Where the case law differs is whether the disclosure actually produces a harm that must be remedied by awarding a new trial. That's the difference between our argument prior to and our argument before this court now, our argument against the interlocutory appeal. But the interlocutory appeal having been accepted, the people urge this court to adopt the position of multiple courts, state courts, and the federal jurisdiction that a defendant has the right to apply to a court in an ex parte hearing and to have an ex parte hearing free from the influence or an adversarial hearing with prosecution to justify to the court why expert funds are necessary. What the prosecution and the government is asking for is simply notice that that hearing or the application has been made. In that application and notice, we are not asking that the defense counsel reveal trial strategy. We are not asking that defense counsel reveal the motivation behind requesting the expert, the expert's area of expertise, or the person or individual sought to be relied upon against expertise. I want to bring up... What about Ms. Zona's argument that

speaker: roberttorres
text: just the mere disclosure of the fact they sought an expert even without identifying the subject area or any of the areas that she suggested you're not asking for would give some advantage to the government and they'd be able to make that argument at trial that they sought an expert and that expert

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: didn't testify? I don't believe that we would have a relevancy ability to make that argument at trial to reference a witness who was consulted by defense counsel but then produced no evidence whatsoever during the course of the trial. Defense counsel may seek the influence of an expert or the information provided by an expert. They do not vet expert. If that expert under the rules of evidence here in Guam produces a report, then we are entitled to that report under the discovery rules under Title, I believe it's Chapter 8 of the Guam Code. I think that that leads me directly into my next point. Disclosure of strategy pre-trial is not inherently a violation of the attorney-client privilege between a criminal defendant and a criminal defense attorney. We have multiple instances where the law requires a defense attorney to reveal witnesses, defense strategy. If there is a report, the prosecution upon motion is entitled to that expert report prior to the trial and I think that that's essential here because under counsel's approach, this is an all or nothing take it or leave it approach. The people are simply asking that our right and our interest, which has been recognized by the court in Ake and the court in Louisiana in the Touche case and the court again in State v. Bright, I believe in Georgia, that the government has an interest in monitoring the expenditure of taxpayer funds. In this, does it make a difference

speaker: roberttorres
text: that Ms. Zona points out that the judicial counsel here has responsibility for the indigent defense funds and the judicial client services funds is separate from the government of Guam general fund accounts? So what is the interest of the prosecution in protecting the fisks, so to speak, as you argued, when it's the judiciary already who's responsible for that and not the executive branch?

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: In each of the cases that I cited to the judiciary is administering the funds that counsel says are being administered under a different, the source of the taxpayer dollars and the way that the taxpayer dollars are doled out doesn't diminish the government's interest in another branch of government doling out taxpayer funds unless the funds are generated independently of taxes, which the judiciary does not have a tax authority in and of itself. The legislature and the executive have a right under our separation of powers authority to have some kind of monitoring authority or some interest in how those funds are dealt out, which is why I believe one of the reasons that when counsel applies for indigency, the prosecution is noticed of it right away. We don't have a separate ex parte hearing for every defendant that comes before the superior court of the magistrate's court where the magistrate independently interviews that individual to find out whether or not they are entitled to indigent funds. That is put on the record and that goes before the people. Does it matter, Mr. Luther, that there are

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: inherent restrictions in the use of these funds? There's a cap of $1,500 that can be billed towards securing an expert witness. I'm just trying to understand what is it that the government can contribute to the judiciary in the interest of being vigilant and not have taxpayers' funds being unnecessarily wasted. What is it that the government, if they're entitled, as you argue, to notice so that the people can make sure that the judiciary is properly expending these limited taxpayer funds regardless of the source of how it's raised. What insight can you provide to the trial court that the trial court may not already be mindful

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: of? The insight is the notice is the right from what I see under the case law. The government's interest, while it may not be the most overwhelming interest and counsel may not find it a compelling interest, the courts have recognized that the government has an interest in how the taxpayer dollars are spent. The government's solution in this case is to thread the needle, so to speak, to balance the interest of the defendant and protecting his defense strategy prior to trial and then also weighing that against the government's interest in having some kind of notification so that taxpayer funds are not doled out completely in secret. Under defense counsel's argument or appellant counsel's argument, the doling out of every application for an indigent defendant would be secret and it would remain secret even after the trial has concluded. How those funds, but at least with notice, the government is kept at least on the surface in the loop and that we're aware of the numerosity if not the substance of applications for expert counsel. How we would proceed if the government found that there was some kind of maybe abuse or excessive application in this case, I think that that's an area that we would proceed to and it's an extreme, but it is something that government has an interest in and I do not believe, and the people have argued in our brief, that by allowing us simply notice that an application has been made, not even the outcome of that application or the procedure, simply allowing us notice does not violate a defendant's right to keep his defense strategy secret. I think it balances the interest of the government against the defendant and we submit that that is the proper course that the court should take. It recognizes the government's interest and it recognizes the defense interest. I do want to clear... What about the

speaker: roberttorres
text: public defender's request for equity? If we are going to require them to disclose a retention of an expert even without the subject area, the government should be bound by the same requirement and that currently the government is not burdened by that requirement.

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: I'm glad that you brought that up, Justice Torres, because I am honestly a bit confused as to counsel's argument on this point. If I, as a criminal prosecutor, discuss a case with an expert witness or a witness within expertise, my discussion with that expert is subject to discovery under Brady and its progeny. My understanding is that I can't keep that expert discussion a secret. If I go out into the field and I discuss with a witness or I have a witness come into my office and I discuss procedure, I have to document and send to counsel notice that the meeting to discuss procedure, not substantive issues, just procedure with that witness occurred and disclose that information to counsel. My understanding is that while there may not be any specific rule in Guam law or under the Guam rules of evidence, Brady and the common law require that I disclose that information to counsel. I've done this multiple times where I've spoken... Isn't that only if it's exculpatory?

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: If, for example, the medical examiner boosts your evidence in your case,

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: you don't have to disclose that, do you? Let's see. I assume that if a medical examiner were to issue an autopsy that's advantageous to the prosecution, I believe that failure to turn over the autopsy prior to trial of the report... First of all, that would be an expert report. I believe the rules would require that we disclose that anyway. But let's assume that there is no statutory requirement under Guam law and no Guam rule of evidence that requires no case law. I believe Brady would actually cover the requirement to turn over a medical examiner's report because it could lead to exculpatory evidence under those circumstances. If I have a substantive discussion with an expert outside of the case, my belief is that I have to turn that information over under U.S. Constitution, under discovery rules. Whether or not Guam law addresses that. I was a little bit confused. I do not believe that a prosecutor has the right to consult with an expert completely ex parte to expend taxpayer funds to receive a report or an evaluation by that expert and then not disclose that information.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Let me just... To me, this is a timing issue is the way I'm seeing it. I mean, it's obvious that pretrial when a court has set the time periods in which these experts reports and have to be provided if they have been intended to be used at trial. speaker: jeremiahluther
text: provide notice to the defendant? Well, if the government is considering, I believe that would be... speaker: jeremiahluther
text: I don't believe the government can retain an expert without a government expense. So I believe in every case where the government again goes out to solicit an expert and actually retains them outside of the areas such as the medical examiner, which we do not have to retain, but we exert very little control over the medical examiner and the medical examiner's office and methods by which the medical examiner draws his conclusion. speaker: philipcarbullido

speaker: philipcarbullido

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: she is contemplating for that service. If Ms. Zona and I were on equal footing as representatives of a governmental entity, I would concede the point. text: Justice Merriman, if I understand your question, I don't want to take up too much time. I would rephrase the question as whether or not the disadvantage in those disparate circumstances or those different circumstances actually leads to real prejudice to the defendant, because I think that in any criminal case, whether a defendant has a private attorney or whether the defendant is given a public defender in each of those cases.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: I'm speaking of court-appointed private counsel.

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: So we have an indigent defendant. I understand your question now. Again, the people's position would be that notice of the request does not prejudice the defendant sufficient that he is deprived of a fair trial or that compromises attorney-client privilege to the extent that the defendant cannot have the free communication with his attorney that law is designed to give him. In those circumstances, in your situation where a court-appointed attorney has to apply for services for an investigator, I would find it confusing as to why a court-appointed attorney who does not have an investigator already on staff would believe that the application for an investigator, which I wouldn't expect that attorney to have in the first place, I think under appellant counsel's approach, that application would need to be in secret as well. I cannot see the prejudice to defendants such that it would deprive him of a fair trial or that it would violate attorney-client privilege in light of the other disclosures that the law requires defense counsel to make already. To me, the revealing of potential witnesses and an expert report, very few but substantive disclosures that the law requires defense counsel to make are far more revealing of trial strategy, and these are again before trial. Disclosures that a defense counsel is required to make are far more revealing of trial strategy, and our courts have sustained that that is not a violation of defendants' rights.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: My other question is, an attorney, a defense attorney has the obligation to meet the discovery requirements if they decide they're going to use the expert, but shouldn't they have the right if the expert's advice is the fingerprints are clearly the defendant's or the DNA results can't be challenged, they've been done properly, the results are foolproof. speaker: jeremiahluther
text: options? As a prosecutor, I'm not sure how I would be aware that the defense counsel has what the results of any expert analysis would be if defense counsel does not turn that information over to me. So if defense counsel doesn't reveal the identity of a defendant either through statutory discovery rules because they simply do not wish to use the expert witness at trial or the report of the expert witness at trial that the information disclosed, then I'm not entitled to that information. And under the government's proposal before the court today, I still wouldn't be entitled to that information. Simply notice that an application for a witness had been made in the past at some point during the pretrial procedures. That's the only notice that I would have under the government's proposal. But again, defense counsel and I are not very far away on this belief that defense counsel is not required to disclose the strategy behind the application for an expert witness. People believe that the government's interest, which I am bound to represent, is simply to notice that an application has been made so that we can monitor in some form or fashion the dispensation of taxpayer-derived funds.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: You don't trust the judges to do that?

speaker: jeremiahluther
text: Your Honor, it is, I think, a principle of our three-part governmental democracy system that the executive branch checks the judiciary, the judiciary checks the legislative and the executive. So while I may not have a specific example where I don't, I can point to a court or a judicial officer where I don't trust them in the expiration or the dispensation of funds, that doesn't mean that we won't have that situation in the future and it doesn't negate the executive branch's obligation to monitor the dispensation of taxpayer dollars. Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Justice.
